entities.name: Corrado Caracciolo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Corrado Caracciolo (b. 1350, Naples – d. 1411-02-24, Rome) was a prominent Italian cardinal and administrator whose ecclesiastical career unfolded during the tumultuous period of the Western Schism. Hailing from the influential Caracciolo family of Naples, his life and decisions were inextricably linked to the struggle for papal legitimacy that fractured the Catholic Church for nearly four decades. His ascent through the ranks of the Church, marked by appointments as Bishop of Monopoli and later Archbishop of Mileto, positioned him at the heart of the political and religious machinations that defined late medieval Europe.

Caracciolo's most significant involvement came with his participation in the Council of Pisa in 1409. This council, convened by cardinals from both the Roman and Avignon obediences, aimed to resolve the schism by deposing both Pope Gregory XII (Roman) and Antipope Benedict XIII (Avignon) and electing a new, universally recognized pontiff. Caracciolo, having been elevated to cardinal by Antipope Alexander V at Pisa, actively supported this third, Pisan line of popes. His actions reflected the widespread desire for Church unity, even as the Pisan solution inadvertently complicated matters by introducing a third claimant to the papacy.

His legacy is thus tied to the prolonged and ultimately unsuccessful efforts to heal the Western Schism through conciliar means prior to the more decisive Council of Constance. While the Council of Pisa failed to achieve its immediate goal of unification, Caracciolo’s administrative contributions and his steadfast support for the conciliar movement represented a significant current within the Church hierarchy that sought reform and resolution. His career exemplifies the profound challenges faced by churchmen navigating a period of unprecedented internal division, where loyalty to a particular pope often clashed with the broader imperative of Christian unity.
